newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria wheat trade paralysed by currency fall.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria wheat trade paralysed by currency fall.

text.p: Bulgaria's Sofia Commodity Exchange (SCE) said the latest fall of the lev against the dollar had paralysed wheat trade this week.
SCE deputy chairman Hristo Milenkov told a news conference on Friday that no deals had been struck at this week's session as buyers had been reluctant to raise their lev-denominated bids.

"Buyers' bids remained unchanged from last week's 231,000 levs ex-works per tonne and no deals were struck after sellers, concerned by the latest fall of the lev against the dollar, refused to negotiate in lev-denominated prices," Milenkov said.

Bulgaria chose the mark as anchor currency and pegged the lev at 1,000 to the mark. A currency board system, requiring levs in circulation be covered by foreign exchange reserves, was introduced on July 1.
"Sellers lowered their prices to $140 per tonne ex-works this week from $150 last week as wheat output is seen rising and they were testing the market," Milenkov said.

The farm ministry said on Tuesday Bulgaria had so far harvested 1.453 million tonnes of wheat from 36.35 percent of the sown area, with an average yield of 3.26 tonnes per hectare, higher than the previously estimated two tonnes.
At this level Bulgaria may harvest 3.994 million tonnes of wheat from a total of 1.225 million ha sown, up from the 2.4 million tonnes estimated by the ministry in May.
The country's annual consumption is estimated at 1.6 million tonnes of bread wheat and 800,000 tonnes of feed wheat.
Bulgaria has to export some 232,000 tonnes of wheat this year under contracts agreed earlier this year to offset bread shortages.
Milenkov said Bulgarian traders expected higher wheat prices on the international market due to recent flooding in central Europe.

"Bulgarian traders should follow the international wheat market trends, which will depend on possible grain shortages in central European countries as the floods have seriously affected this year's crop there," Milenkov said.

"On the other hand private bread producers are negotiating imports from neighbouring Yugoslavia and Romania as wheat ex-works prices there are under $100 per tonne and transport costs are relatively low," he added.
Private bread producers meet half of the domestic market's needs, the Union of Private Bread Producers said on Thursday.

The minimum wheat purchase price is set at 230 marks per tonne for this year's crop in a bid to secure the country's grain ballance after excessive wheat exports two years ago and a bad harvest in 1996 caused acute grain shortages earlier this year.
An export fee of 15 percent of international wheat prices has been also set in a bid to curb exports.
